literal: The Chancellor and Prince of Gaoyang, Yong, though his position outweighed Cha's, yet greatly feared and dreaded him; he wished to speak to Emperor Xiaozong but had no occasion.
idiomatic: Chancellor Yuan Yong, prince of Gaoyang, outranked Yuan Cha yet feared him deeply and could find no opening to warn Emperor Xiaozong.

literal: It happened that the empress dowager and Xiaozong toured the Luo River southward; Yong invited them, and the imperial carriage thereupon visited Yong's residence.
idiomatic: When the empress dowager and Xiaozong went south along the Luo, Yong invited them and the court called at his house.

literal: As day drew toward dusk, Xiaozong and the empress dowager reached Yong's inner chamber; attendants were not admitted, and they settled the plot against Cha.
idiomatic: At dusk Xiaozong and the dowager entered Yong's private rooms alone with him and fixed the plan to bring Cha down.

literal: Later, when Yong followed Xiaozong to audience with the empress dowager, he advanced and said: "Your servant does not worry over the realm's rebels—only over Yuan Cha.
idiomatic: Later, attending Xiaozong at audience with the dowager, Yong said, "I fear no rebels in the empire—only Yuan Cha.

literal: Why?
idiomatic: Why so?

literal: Cha holds overall command of the forbidden guard; all troops belong to him;
idiomatic: He commands the palace guard and every soldier answers to him;

literal: his father leads a host of a million men, glaring like a tiger at the capital's west;
idiomatic: his father leads a million men and eyes the western approaches to the capital;

literal: his younger brother is area commander, commanding the forces of the three Qi.
idiomatic: his brother is area commander over all three Qi provinces.

literal: If Yuan Cha has no heart for it, so be it; if he has a heart for it, how will the holy court resist?
idiomatic: If Yuan Cha means no harm, well and good—but if he does, what can the court oppose him with?

literal: Though Cha says he will not rebel, who has seen his heart?
idiomatic: He may deny rebellion, but who can read his mind?

literal: Yet one cannot but fear.
idiomatic: Fear him we must nonetheless.

literal: " The empress dowager said: "So.
idiomatic: " The dowager said, "True.

literal: If Lord Yuan is loyal to the court and has no rebellious heart, why not remove this command of the guards and let him assist government with other offices?
idiomatic: If Yuan is loyal and plots no revolt, why keep him as commander of the guards—give him other posts and let him aid government that way?

literal: " Hearing this, Cha was greatly afraid; he removed his cap and begged to be released.
idiomatic: " Cha heard and was terrified; he doffed his cap and asked to resign.

literal: Cha was then made Grand General Who Conquers on Horseback, Bearer of the Triple Staff, Director of the Secretariat, Palace Attendant, and Director of the Left and Right.
idiomatic: He was made grand general who conquers on horseback, bearer of the triple staff, director of the secretariat, palace attendant, and director of the left and right.

literal: Though Cha had lost military power, he still held overall charge within and without and did not at all expect grounds for dismissal.
idiomatic: Stripped of the army, he still ran court and camp alike and never imagined he could be removed.

literal: Later, when Cha lodged out overnight, his palace attendant post was removed.
idiomatic: When he stayed out overnight, his palace attendant title was taken away.

literal: At dawn he wished to enter the palace; the gatekeepers would not admit him.
idiomatic: At dawn he tried to enter the palace; the gates refused him.

literal: Shortly he was struck from the rolls and made a commoner.
idiomatic: Soon he was erased from the registers and reduced to commoner status.

literal: Earlier, the Prince of Xianyang, Xi, had been executed for treason; his son Shu fled to Xiao Yan, and Yan enfeoffed him Prince of Ye.
idiomatic: Earlier Prince Xi of Xianyang was executed for treason; his son Shu fled to Xiao Yan, who made him prince of Ye.

literal: After Fa Seng's rebellion, Shu sent a letter to the hundred officials and the nobility, saying:
idiomatic: After Fa Seng rebelled, Shu wrote the chief ministers and officials:

literal: The house of Wei is ill-fated; wicked eunuchs monopolize the court, the altars teeter on the brink, and the royal tassel hangs by a thread unfit for comparison.
idiomatic: Wei is ill-starred: vicious minions hold the court, the altars totter, and the royal fringe dangles by a thread.

literal: Yuan Cha is treacherous, cruel, and wolfish, not fit for human society; of distant lineage in the clan registers, he had no standing reputation, yet solely because of kinship with the empress dowager he was early raised to favor.
idiomatic: Yuan Cha is treacherous, cruel, and wolfish—no fit member of society; a distant name on the clan rolls without repute, he rose only through the dowager's kin.

literal: He never cherished kindness; openly he turned to bite back, indulging this perversity, and men and spirits alike rage.
idiomatic: He never repaid kindness; he bit the hand that fed him and flaunted rebellion until men and gods alike raged.

literal: Of late all that the borderlands report says: Cha's heart is wolfish and scorpion-poisoned; leaning on power, he grows daily;
idiomatic: Lately every report from the provinces says his heart is wolfish and scorpion-venomed and that he swells daily on borrowed power;

literal: bearing insult while practicing flattery and fraud, more so with each passing day and month.
idiomatic: he swallows insult while piling on flattery and fraud, worse with every passing day.

literal: A heart without a lord is no longer a matter of a single day;
idiomatic: Disloyalty to the throne is no new thing with him;

literal: usurpation and coercion will be enacted morning or evening.
idiomatic: seizure of the throne may come at any dawn or dusk.

literal: Moreover one hears that names issue from trust, trust governs righteousness; hidden ailments of mountains and rivers are still not put into names—when the army was formed, omens of disorder appeared; a great lord not ministering to his prince—seek it in the histories, and it has always been so.
idiomatic: Moreover names must carry trust and trust must bind duty: even hidden ills of land and river are not lightly named—when armies form, chaos is foretold; a great lord who will not serve his prince has precedent on every page of history.

literal: Yuan Cha's original name was Yecha; his younger brother Luo's true name was Luosha; Yecha and Luosha are demons that devour men—not unless black wind meets them is it like drifting and falling.
idiomatic: Yuan Cha was originally named Yecha and his brother Luo was truly Luosha—night-demons and rakshasas that devour men, swept away only when black wind strikes.

literal: Alas, the realm of Wei!
idiomatic: Alas for Wei!

literal: Part from these two calamities.
idiomatic: Free yourselves of these two scourges.

literal: A wicked tree, a stolen spring—do not rest, do not drink;
idiomatic: Under a wicked tree, at a stolen spring—neither rest nor drink;

literal: a name of victory, a title of owl—do not enter, do not act.
idiomatic: a triumphant name, an owl's title—neither enter nor act.

literal: How much more when brothers bear these names, proclaiming power to devour things; exposed to the sun long ago, one now believes these words.
idiomatic: How much worse when brothers bear such names, advertising their taste for flesh—the sun has exposed them long since, and the omen is believed.

literal: Moreover the empress dowager suffers secret shame, the succeeding lord is covered in dust; casting off rank and brandishing weapons, speaking of plotting against the royal house—not today alone—what sort of minister is this!
idiomatic: Moreover the dowager suffers outrage in seclusion and the reigning lord is dishonored; casting off office and taking up arms while plotting the royal house—not since yesterday—what minister is this!

literal: You worthies perhaps inherit virtue generation after generation, or succeed one another as generals and ministers, or receive office through many reigns, or hold posts at the pivot of power, or are kin by marriage beyond others, or bear loyalty and righteousness—bowing brows and turning hands, constrained by fierce might, your ministerial integrity unfulfilled, you toil in vain.
idiomatic: Some of you inherit virtue for generations, some fill general and ministerial posts in succession, some serve many reigns, some sit at the hinges of power, some are marriage kin beyond the ordinary, some are sworn to loyalty—yet you bow and yield to brutal force, your service unperformed, your labor wasted.

literal: One also hears that since Cha monopolized government the myriad people have parted from virtue; added to yearly disasters and pestilence, year after year flood and drought, oxen and horses perish and fall, mulberry and catalpa scorch dry, famine follows famine, hunger's hue fills the roads, strange calamities proclaim reproof, and all men sigh.
idiomatic: It is also said that since Cha seized power the people have turned from virtue; floods, drought, and plague year on year kill cattle and horses, wither the mulberry fields, and leave famine upon famine until hunger colors every road—omens cry out and all men sigh.

literal: Northwest of Chan and Jian, Qiang and Rong rampage;
idiomatic: Northwest of Chan and Jian the Qiang and Rong run riot;

literal: left and right of Si and Bian, garrison grain-transport troops wander displaced.
idiomatic: along the Si and Bian the garrison and transport troops scatter in exile.

literal: Added to this, loyal worthies are carved apart and the imperial clan exterminated; pity this native state—overthrown in a morning.
idiomatic: Loyal men are cut down and the imperial clan wiped out; pity the homeland—overturned in a single morning.

literal: Now I have led the army and will remove the evil at the ruler's side.
idiomatic: I now lead troops to purge the evil beside the throne.

literal: In this petty breast I hope only that caps and shoes may find their place, that the great villain share the punishment all must inflict, and that Wei's sacrifices suffer no neglect of ritual.
idiomatic: In my humble wish, may rank and station be restored, the arch-villain share the death all demand, and Wei's rites suffer no lapse.

literal: Cha was hated by near and far to this degree.
idiomatic: Such was the hatred Yuan Cha drew from every quarter.

literal: Afterward Empress Dowager Ling said to attendants: "Liu Teng and Yuan Cha once begged me for iron tallies, hoping not to die; I was fortunate not to grant them.
idiomatic: Later Empress Dowager Hu told her attendants, "Liu Teng and Yuan Cha once begged me for iron tallies promising they would not die; I was lucky to refuse.

literal: " Secretariat Gentleman Han Zixi said: "It concerns killing and keeping alive—how could one reckon grant or refusal?
idiomatic: " Secretariat gentleman Han Zixi said, "Life and death were at stake—what matter grant or refusal?

literal: Though Your Majesty did not grant them then, why not kill them today?
idiomatic: You did not grant them then—why spare them now?

literal: " Empress Dowager Ling was disconcerted.
idiomatic: " The dowager was unsettled.

literal: Before long someone reported that Cha and his younger brother Zhao plotted rebellion, wishing to have their faction attack the counties near the capital, break markets and burn town and suburb to alarm within and without, first sending his younger cousin Hongye to lead surrendered households of the six garrisons in revolt at Ding Province, and also having men incite the barbarians of Luyang to harass Yique—Cha and his brothers as inner responders.
idiomatic: Soon someone accused Cha and his brother Zhao of plotting revolt: their faction would strike counties near the capital, sack markets and burn suburbs to shock court and country, while Cha's cousin Hongye would raise the six-garrison surrenderers at Ding Province and agents would stir the Luyang tribes against Yique—with the brothers as insiders.

literal: The rising was set for a day; his handwriting was obtained.
idiomatic: A date was fixed for the uprising and his own hand was captured.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling, because of the marriage tie to her younger sister, could not bear to decide at once.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Hu, for her sister's sake, hesitated to act.

literal: Yellow Gate Gentleman Li Yanzhi said: "Yuan Cha's crimes fill the near and far—how can they be allowed to linger and confuse eyes and ears?
idiomatic: Yellow gate gentleman Li Yanzhi said, "Yuan Cha's crimes are known everywhere—how can execution wait and confuse the court?

literal: " Yellow Gate Xu He hastened forward wishing to remonstrate, hesitated, and did not dare.
idiomatic: " Yellow gate Xu He stepped forward to object, wavered, and held his tongue.

literal: The assembled ministers pressed unceasingly; Xiaozong also spoke for it, and the empress dowager then assented.
idiomatic: The ministers pressed hard; Xiaozong spoke too, and the dowager consented.

literal: Thereupon Cha and his younger brother Zhao were both granted death at home.
idiomatic: Cha and his brother Zhao were then ordered to die at home.

literal: The empress dowager still because of her younger sister posthumously restored Cha as Palace Attendant, Grand General Who Conquers on Horseback, Bearer of the Triple Staff, Director of the Secretariat, and Inspector of Ji Province.
idiomatic: For her sister's sake the dowager still posthumously restored Cha as palace attendant, grand general who conquers on horseback, bearer of the triple staff, director of the secretariat, and inspector of Ji.

literal: Cha's son Liang inherited his grandfather's title.
idiomatic: Cha's son Liang inherited his grandfather's enfeoffment.

literal: When Qi received the mandate, by precedent he was demoted.
idiomatic: When Qi took the mandate, titles were reduced by precedent.

literal: Cha's eldest son by a concubine, Zhi, [10] Secretariat Gentleman.
idiomatic: Cha's eldest son by a concubine, Zhi, served as secretariat gentleman.[10]

literal: After Cha's death he fled to Xiao Yan.
idiomatic: When Cha died he took refuge with Xiao Yan.

literal: Cha's younger brother Luo, styled Zhonggang, was known for frugality and plainness.
idiomatic: Cha's brother Luo, styled Zhonggang, was noted for plain frugality.

literal: He began office as aide in the Ministry of Works, transferred to chief clerk in the Ministry of Education, and held Director of Imperial Viands, Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant, and Regular Cavalier Attendant.
idiomatic: He entered service as aide in the ministry of works, became chief clerk in the ministry of education, and held director of imperial viands, supernumerary cavalier attendant, and regular cavalier attendant.

literal: Though father and elder brothers were noble and flourishing, he emptied himself in modesty and deferral, earnest in receiving others.
idiomatic: Though his father and brothers were at the height of power, he remained humble and courteous in all dealings.

literal: He was promoted General Who Pacifies the East and Inspector of Qing Province.
idiomatic: He was promoted to general who pacifies the east and inspector of Qing.

literal: When Cha monopolized the court, Luo's fame tilted the four seas; at the time men of talent and name—Wang Yuanjing, Xing Zicai, Li Jiang, and others—were all his guests and followed him to the land of Qing.
idiomatic: While Cha ruled the court, Luo's renown swayed the empire; Wang Yuanjing, Xing Zicai, Li Jiang, and other leading men were his clients and traveled with him to Qing.

literal: At the time Xiao Yan sent generals to raid the border; Luo was made General Who Comforts the Army and Area Commander of the military affairs of Qing, Guang, and Southern Qing provinces.
idiomatic: When Xiao Yan's generals raided the frontier, Luo was made general who comforts the army and area commander over Qing, Guang, and southern Qing.

literal: When his provincial term ended he entered the capital as Director of the Imperial Clan.
idiomatic: Leaving the province, he entered court as director of the imperial clan.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaozhuang's reign he was made Right Vice Director of the Secretariat and Grand Ambassador of the Eastern Route.
idiomatic: At Emperor Xiaozhuang's accession he became right vice director of the secretariat and grand ambassador of the eastern route.

literal: In the time of the Outgoing Emperor he was promoted Director of the Secretariat; shortly he was made Bearer of the Staff, Grand General Who Conquers on Horseback, Bearer of the Triple Staff with an office equal to the Three Excellencies, and Inspector of Liang Province.
idiomatic: Under the outgoing emperor he became director of the secretariat, then bearer of the staff, grand general who conquers on horseback, bearer of the triple staff with an office equal to the three excellencies, and inspector of Liang.

literal: Luo was timid and weak; at the beginning of Emperor Xiaojing, Xiao Yan sent generals to press the siege, and Luo surrendered the province.
idiomatic: Timid by nature, at the start of Emperor Xiaojing's reign he surrendered Liang when Xiao Yan's generals besieged it.

literal: After Cha's death, Luo forced Cha's wife; men of the time reviled him.
idiomatic: After Cha died, Luo forced Cha's wife—a deed men of the time despised.

literal: Some say it was a plan to save his life.
idiomatic: Some said it was a stratagem to save his own life.

literal: Luo's younger brother Shuang, styled Jingzhe.
idiomatic: Luo's brother Shuang was styled Jingzhe.

literal: In youth he was sharp and alert, especially favored by his father.
idiomatic: Clever and quick from youth, he was his father's favorite.

literal: Upon leaving the sack he was Secretariat Gentleman, and was gradually promoted Attendant of the Yellow Gate and Grand Master of Splendid Brightness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
idiomatic: On first appointment he was secretariat gentleman, then rose to attendant of the yellow gate and grand master of splendid brightness with golden seal and purple ribbon.

literal: In the second year of Yongxi he died; he was posthumously granted Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander of the military affairs of Jing, Qi, and Qin provinces, General of the Guards, Left Vice Director of the Secretariat, and Inspector of Qin Province, with posthumous title Yi.
idiomatic: He died in Yongxi year 2 and was posthumously made bearer of the staff, area commander of Jing, Qi, and Qin, general of the guards, left vice director of the secretariat, and inspector of Qin, with posthumous title Yi.

literal: Shuang's son Delong, at the end of Wuding, was Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
idiomatic: Shuang's son Delong was junior mentor of the heir apparent at the end of Wuding.

literal: Shuang's younger brother Man, at the end of Wuding, was Director of the Imperial Household.
idiomatic: Shuang's brother Man was director of the imperial household at the end of Wuding.

literal: Zhao, styled Jingyong, Attendant Within the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: Zhao, styled Jingyong, was attendant within the yellow gate.

literal: Together with his elder brother Cha he was executed for the same crime.
idiomatic: He was executed with his brother Cha for the same offense.

literal: A younger cousin, Luohou, at the time of the move to Luoyang, because the ancestral tombs lay in the north, then made his home in Changping commandery of Yan Province.
idiomatic: A younger cousin, Luohou, when the capital moved to Luoyang kept his household in Changping commandery of Yan because the family tombs lay in the north.

literal: Within, his wealth was abundant; he took only what pleased his mind as fitting and did not enter the capital.
idiomatic: Wealthy at home, he lived as inclination dictated and never entered the capital.

literal: When guests came and went he always sent them off with generous gifts; dominating the north with force, he had a great reputation.
idiomatic: Guests always left with rich parting gifts; he dominated the north and enjoyed wide renown.

literal: When Cha's power was heavy, because Luohou took no pleasure in entering office, he was appointed in place as Administrator of Changping.
idiomatic: While Cha held power, Luohou was made administrator of Changping because he would not take office willingly.

literal: At the end of Zhenguang the rebel Da'e Fobao seized the commandery and Luohou was killed.
idiomatic: At the end of Zhenguang the rebel Da'e Fobao took the commandery and killed him.

literal: His son Jingzun, Direct Attendant of the Inner Quarters, Vice Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
idiomatic: His son Jingzun was direct attendant of the inner quarters and vice director of the imperial ancestral temple.

literal: The historiographer says: The owl-mirror is a creature heaven truly engenders; knowing its mother it forgets its father—also a kind of bird and beast; Yuan Shao was such a man—is he not worse than this!
idiomatic: The historiographer writes: Heaven breeds the owl-mirror, a beast that knows its mother and forgets its father; Yuan Shao was such a man—worse still than that creature.

literal: From the Prince of Yangping downward, years were cut short in youth; heroic talent and martial stratagem did not show in their time.
idiomatic: From the prince of Yangping down, lives ended young; talent and arms never found their hour.

literal: The two princes Jing and Jian were foremost in reputation for their age.
idiomatic: Princes Jing and Jian led their generation in renown.

literal: Jian already had a voice; Hun too was regarded as material.
idiomatic: Jian already had a name; Hun too was seen as promising.

literal: Xiao bore Gaozu's favor and in succession received office in the Taihe era; had they lacked talent, could name and rank have reached them in vain?
idiomatic: Xiao enjoyed Gaozu's favor and served through the Taihe years—without ability, rank and fame would not have come to them empty-handed.

literal: Cha climbed by favor and private ties; his wisdom was small yet his schemes large, his burden heavy yet his talent weak—he thereupon threw the realm into chaos; to die yet preserve sacrifice—is that not fortune!
idiomatic: Cha rose on private favor: small wit, grand plots, heavy trust, weak talent—he threw the realm into chaos; to die yet keep his line in the sacrifices—was that not luck!

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Administrator of Donghai concurrently Defender of the Tongyu Garrison. The Palace edition's textual verification, citing Hanshu juan 28A, Treatise on Geography, Upper, Donghai commandery, Siwu, holds that "Tong" is a corruption of "[siwu mountain character]."
idiomatic: "Administrator of Donghai, concurrently defender of Tongyu garrison": the Palace edition's Kaozheng, citing Hanshu 28A (Geography, upper) on Donghai commandery's Siwu, takes Tong as a corruption of the Siwu graph.

literal: Commentary: Shuijing zhu juan 26, Shu River, has "Mount Siwu" and "the old city of Siwu county."
idiomatic: Note: Shuijing zhu 26 (Shu River) mentions Mount Siwu and the old city of Siwu county.

literal: The character "Tong" is corrupt; the verification is correct.
idiomatic: Tong is a scribal error; the emendation stands.

literal: Fa Seng killed the Mobile Corps commander Gao Liang. In all editions "Liang" is written "Mo"; the Palace edition, according to juan 9, Annals of Emperor Xiaozong, first month of Xiaochang year 1 recording this affair and juan 57, Biography of Gao You, appended biography of Gao Liang, changes it to "Liang."
idiomatic: "Fa Seng killed mobile corps commander Gao Liang": witnesses read Liang as Mo; the Palace edition, from juan 9 (Xiaozong, Xiaochang 1.1) and juan 57 (Gao You, appended Gao Liang), restores Liang.

literal: Commentary: Beishi juan 16, Biographies of the Seven Princes of Emperor Daowu, also writes "Liang."
idiomatic: Note: Beishi 16 (Daowu's seven princes) also has Liang.

literal: The character "Mo" is corrupt; now follow the Palace edition.
idiomatic: Mo is wrong; follow the Palace edition.

literal: In the time of Emperor Shizu. Zhang Senkai says: "Above it already says 'in the time of Gaozu,' so here it cannot say 'Shizu'; 'zu' is probably a corruption of 'zong.'"
idiomatic: "In the time of Emperor Shizu": Zhang Senkai argues that since the text already says "in Gaozu's time," Shizu cannot stand here—zu likely corrupts zong.
